extracted.intended_audience: genre analysts, pragmatics/linguistics researchers, and public-relations practitioners interested in press-release effectiveness
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing press releases that balance informative and promotional functions so journalists will 'pick up' and reuse material. Focuses on textual features and pragmatic strategies that codify the hybrid informative/promotional genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person reportive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Release should read as a journalistic report on the issuer, not as the issuer's first-person speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formulations like 'Acme Corporation announced today that...' rather than 'We are pleased to announce...'. Avoid first-person plural voice; present claims as reported facts to increase journalist uptake. Anti-pattern: marketing-style 'we're thrilled' leads to sub-editor deletion or non-pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported-speech promotional payload
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional claims should be packaged as attributed quotes from named individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place promotional evaluations in quoted attributions (e.g., "'This is a transformative moment for the industry,' said CEO Y"). Rationale: sub-editors more readily preserve quoted promotional material than un-attributed praise. Anti-pattern: embedding promotional claims in the release's un-attributed voice makes them likely to be stripped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information-density per sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Each sentence should advance the news; high 'facts per sentence' improves chances of surviving editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor sentences that carry verifiable facts, dates, figures, or news events rather than rhetorical flourishes. Catenaccio shows releases with higher information density are transformed more intact into news copy. Scoring note: measure by how many discrete news-relevant facts a sentence contributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional company-description ('About Acme') belongs in a clearly demarcated boilerplate block at the bottom — never woven into the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the lead strictly news-focused; place background/promotional material in a labeled 'About' section. Anti-pattern: weaving company puffery into the opening makes the piece read as advertorial and reduces pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic appropriateness (register match)
rubrics_metrics.description: The register should match journalists' expectations: factual, attributable, scannable, and time-stamped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use datelines, clear attributions, timestamps, and a scannable structure so journalists can quickly evaluate newsworthiness. Avoid promotional register or blurred modality. Example features: dateline, short paragraphs, explicit contact block. Receiver-oriented test: would a journalist recognize and classify this as news copy?

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of 'self-praise' lexical bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overuse self-evaluative lexical bundles such as 'leading', 'best-in-class', 'cutting-edge', 'world-class'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lexical-bundle studies show such bundles are often deleted or marked as promotional residue. Replace generic praise with concrete, verifiable descriptors or attribute praise to external sources. Anti-pattern: repetition of marketing superlatives throughout the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability of promotional claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional claims that survive sub-editing are those journalists can verify (e.g., rankings, market-share data with source, awards with dates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including promotional facts, cite sources, provide dates, rankings, or measurable metrics. Unverifiable assertions are likely to be removed. Example: include 'ranked #2 in X by Y research, 2007' rather than 'industry-leading'.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-value primacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The release should be evaluable as news independent of its promotional benefit; if every sentence reads as promotional, the release will be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the lead carries clear news value (timeliness, impact, novelty) that stands alone. Balance is key: the release must serve a news function such that journalists can justify coverage even if the issuer benefits commercially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver-role multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for multiple receivers: journalists (who need copy) and end readers (public on issuer's site); the hybrid release must pass both audiences without slipping into one mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure and language should be suitable for journalistic reuse while still serving secondary public-facing goals. Test: would both a sub-editor and a general reader find the text appropriate? Avoid text that only caters to marketing or only to technical audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre signposting (formal conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe genre conventions (dateline, contact block, headline format, '—END—' marker) so receivers immediately classify the text as a press release rather than an advertorial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include conventional markers that facilitate classification and processing by journalists: clear headline, dateline, contact information, boilerplate, and end marker. Such signposts reduce friction in newsroom adoption and signal the text's intended use.
